title: Discrimination alleged in 2018 deaths of Knapaysweet, Sutherland
subtitle: OHRC announced it has filed an application with the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario alleging discrimination by 'service providers' leading up to deaths
article: On the second anniversary of the deaths of Joey Knapaysweet and Agnes Sutherland, the Ontario Human Rights Commission (OHRC) announced it has filed an application with the Human Rights Tribunal of Ontario (HRTO) alleging discrimination based on Indigenous ancestry by public service providers in Timmins.

"The February 2018 deaths of Joey Knapaysweet and Agnes Sutherland highlight the serious and sometimes tragic result of systemic discrimination against First Nations peoples in Northern Ontario," the OHRC stated in a release. "Both Joey Knapaysweet and Agnes Sutherland traveled to Timmins from Fort Albany First Nation, more than 400 km away, to access health services that were not available in their community. These circumstances left them particularly vulnerable to discrimination."

Yves Massicotte, OHRC spokesman stated in an email to The Daily Press, "The OHRC contends that police and health services did not apply existing best practices to ensure that Indigenous peoples receive substantively equivalent quality of service. The failure of the hospital and police to provide services consistent with these individuals' needs was a factor in their tragic deaths.

"The Ontario Human Rights Code requires that services be provided in an equal way. Substantive equality means that particular needs and circumstances of Indigenous peoples must be taken into account when delivering services. We are concerned on a systemic level about the service providers' ability to understand Indigenous issues and offer services that take them into account."

The service providers cited in the OHRC application to the HRTO include the Timmins Police Service, Timmins and District Hospital and Cochrane District Social Services Administration Board (which provides emergency medical services).

The deaths of Knapaysweet and Sutherland, both unrelated and occurring on a single weekend in February 2018, created a firestorm on local social media with many Indigenous residents expressing their outrage on The Daily Press website and other social media sites, suggesting the deaths were fuelled by racism.

"When I visited Timmins in the weeks after Joey Knapaysweet's and Agnes Sutherland's deaths, many people I spoke to linked their deaths to systemic racism and unequal access to essential services," said OHRC Chief Commissioner Renu Mandhane. "The deaths of two vulnerable people who came to Timmins seeking help should be an impetus for concrete action to advance human rights and reconciliation."
However, when Ontario's Special Investigations Unit looked into the circumstances surrounding the two deaths, the SIU cleared the Timmins Police Service of any wrongdoing.

According to the SIU's report released in March 2019, Knapaysweet, 21, was shot dead on frozen Gillies Lake on the morning Saturday, Feb. 3, when he lunged at a police officer while armed with a kitchen knife.
There is evidence in the SIU report to suggest Knapaysweet was suicidal and intent on provoking police to kill him.
The officer initially tried using a conducted energy weapon (commonly referred to as a Taser) but when that failed to have any effect, the officer pulled out his service revolver.
Knapaysweet ignored demands to drop the knife, came at the officer and the officer fired four times.

The incident at Gillies Lake took place on the morning of that Saturday when police officers were called to the ambulance base on the ground floor of the Cochrane District Social Services Administration Board building, located at 500 Algonquin Blvd.

The other matter investigated by SIU involved Sutherland, 62, a member of Fort Albany First Nation, who had been placed under arrest for uttering threats but died on Sunday, Feb. 4, 2018 of "complications of end-stage diabetic nephropathy in a woman with ischemic heart disease."

She had several serious medical health issues, including kidney failure (for which she required dialysis three times per week), diabetes (which contributed to the amputation of one of her legs) and heart disease, according to the SIU report.
Two days prior to her death, she began to refuse treatment.
Massicotte said, "The HRTO has the power to order specific remedies, in accordance with the Human Rights Code."

The OHRC said it is seeking a "variety of public interest remedies," including requiring the respondents to: engage with Indigenous communities to understand their concerns and needs; Develop policies and provide training to ensure that their services are delivered in a culturally competent and safe manner, free of discrimination; develop a human resources plan to promote and expand the hiring and promotion of Indigenous staff; and collect human rights-based data to identify problems and monitor solutions.

Massicotte said, " The OHRC filed an application to support the Knapaysweet and Sutherland families, and to ensure that the tribunal is able to consider all aspects of systemic discrimination in this case. The particular circumstances of their deaths will come out through the Tribunal hearing process."

He explained, "The HRTO is an independent tribunal that holds hearings and hears evidence and argument, like a court ... The length of time that it takes a matter to be heard and decided can vary greatly."

According to the group's website, the "OHRC acts in the public interest and is committed to ensuring that Indigenous peoples receive equal access to essential services consistent with their unique cultural and language needs, pursuant to the Ontario Human Rights Code and consistent with the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples."
